_meta.coder_notes: Baseline established by reading FY2024 10-K (0001326801-25-000017), FY2025 10-K (0001628280-26-003942), and the Q2 2026 10-Q Commitments & Contingencies note (0001628280-26-050705 / R17.htm). Meta carries a standing generative-AI risk factor in every 10-K (FY2022-FY2025) and every 10-Q from 2023 through Q2 2026 that enumerates: 'harmful or illegal content, accuracy, misinformation and deepfakes (including related to elections), bias, discrimination, toxicity, consumer protection, products liability, intellectual property infringement, defamation, data privacy, cybersecurity,' plus a third-party-misuse clause ('we cannot guarantee that third parties will not use such AI technologies for improper purposes, including through the dissemination of illegal, inaccurate, defamatory or harmful content'). It also carries separate harmful/objectionable-content, content-moderation-failure, and minors/teen-safety risk factors. FTS confirms same-family language is present in a window filing for EVERY incident here. No incident in this batch is NAMED in any Meta filing. Targeted FTS negatives: 'Starbuck' = 0 hits, 'Wongbandue' = 0 hits. 'chatbot' appears in exactly ONE filing (Q2 2026 10-Q) but refers to an EU antitrust interim measure about 'general purpose AI providers using the WhatsApp Business API to provide chatbot services' -- NOT any AI-safety incident here. The only NAMED AI-related litigation in the contingencies note is Kadrey v. Meta (AI-training copyright) and the EU DSA youth proceedings; neither maps to a discrete incident in this batch. Consequently there are no T1 or T2 codes; accounting_channel is null throughout. The contingencies note's accrual language ('accrued significant amounts... reasonable possibility that additional accruals... could be material') is tied to European privacy/competition matters, not these AI incidents.

796.evidence: Q2 2024 10-Q (0001326801-24-000069, filed 2024-08-01) and FY2024 10-K carry harmful/objectionable-content and content-moderation-failure risk factors ('failure to prevent or limit spam or otherwise objectionable content'; risk that we 'take, or fail to take, actions to enforce our policies, that result in our removal of users'). Over-removal of legitimate wildfire emergency posts by automated moderation falls squarely in this same family. Event not named.
specific_queries: baseline: content-moderation/objectionable-content risk factor in FY2024 10-K
796.rationale: Automated content-moderation over-removal error; Meta discloses generic content-moderation and objectionable-content risk but never names discrete moderation-error events. Classic T3.

789.evidence: Same content-moderation/objectionable-content risk factor family in Q2 2024 10-Q (2024-08-01) and FY2024 10-K ('failure to prevent or limit spam or otherwise objectionable content'; enforcement-action risk). 789.rationale: AI moderation false-positive against publishers; covered by generic content/enforcement risk language, not disclosed specifically. T3.

788.evidence: FY2024 10-K minors/teen-safety risk factors (state laws 'restricting our ability to offer services to minors'; Nevada AG teen-encryption action; 'activities that threaten people's safety or well-being... including with respect to younger users' in FY2025 10-K) plus objectionable-content risk. Meta also discloses broad Youth-Related Actions litigation (Social Media Adolescent Addiction MDL; New Mexico/Tennessee AG youth cases) about algorithmic harm to minors -- same family but not a consequence of this specific incident. Event not named.
788.rationale: Algorithmic recommendation of sexual content to teen accounts; same family as disclosed teen-safety risk factors and youth litigation, but the specific WSJ-tested event is not named and the MDL predates it. Conservative T3 (not T2, since the disclosed litigation is not a consequence of this incident).
